Title: Forecasting Extreme Fire Weather across the United States: A Deep Dive with Deep Learning, Uncertainty Quantification, and Explainable AI
Brief Abstract:
The ignition, spread, and intensity of wildfires are driven largely by weather conditions (Jain et al. 2020: https://doi.org/10.1139/er-2020-0019; Liu et al. 2013: https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0055618). Fire weather is usually quantified by indices derived from basic weather variables, such as 2-m temperature/dewpoint, 10-m wind, and precipitation. Hence, the main tool for large-scale prediction of fire weather is numerical weather prediction (NWP). However, NWP models are not specifically tuned for fire weather, leaving room for improvement via post-processing. Also, most NWP models do not provide adequate uncertainty quantification - single-member models provide only one deterministic forecasts, and ensemble models are notoriously underdispersive. Thus, we use machine learning with uncertainty quantification (ML-UQ) to post-process NWP forecasts of fire weather.
Specifically, we post-process Global Forecast System (GFS) forecasts of fire weather at short- to long-range lead times (1, 2, ..., 14 days) across the entire United States, including Alaska and Hawaii. We predict the seven variables making up the widely used Canadian Fire Weather Index System (CFWIS), which quantify fuel moisture in light to heavy fuels, potential fire spread, and potential fire intensity. The seven target variables are the fine-fuel moisture code (FFMC), duff moisture code (DMC), drought code (DC), initial-spread index (ISI), buildup index (BUI), fire-weather index (FWI), and daily severity rating (DSR). Truth labels are computed by applying the CFWIS calculations, codified in the fwi.fbp software package (Wang et al. 2019: https://r-forge.r-project.org/projects/fwi-fbp/), to weather fields from the ECMWF Reanalysis version 5 (ERA5).

Our model is a deep neural network with a modified U-net++ architecture (Zhou et al. 2019: https://doi.org/10.1109/TMI.2019.2959609), taking predictors from five data sources. The first is a GFS-forecast time series of atmospheric state variables (temperature, humidity, wind, and pressure/height) at levels including the surface, 900 hPa, and 700 hPa. The second is a GFS-forecast time series of surface and subsurface moisture - namely soil moisture, accumulated precipitation, and snow depth. The third is a set of time-invariant fields related to terrain - including orographic height, slope, aspect, land/sea mask, etc. The fourth is a lagged time series of truth variables (ERA5-derived CFWIS indices) over the past several days. The fifth and last data source is a forecast time series of the target variables (CFWIS indices), computed by applying fwi.fbp directly to GFS weather fields. This data source also constitutes the baseline (raw fire-weather forecasts), which we compare with forecasts from the U-net++ model. The single U-net++ produces an ensemble forecast of every target variable at every lead time at every grid point.

To suit this particular application, we modify the basic U-net++ methodology as follows. First, we use a custom loss function called the dual-weighted mean squared error (DWMSE) skill score. The "dual-weighted" part emphasizes extreme values of all fire-weather indices, and the baseline for the skill score is the raw GFS forecast valid at the same time. Thus, our loss function emphasizes improvement over the raw GFS, especially for extremes. Second, because two of the target variables are uniquely related to each other - namely, DSR = 0.0272 * FWI1.77 - we enforce this relationship in the model architecture. Third, we use residual prediction, where the U-net++ is tasked only with predicting the difference between the current truth fields (CFWIS indices at forecast-issue time) and those at the valid time (CFWIS indices 1-14 days ahead). Title: Random Forest Model predicting next-hour fire radiative power (FRP) for RAVE FRP and GFS weather variable inputs
Brief Abstract: This Zenodo record provides a trained random forest model (saved as a .sav file) that predicts next-hour Fire Radiative Power (FRP) using inputs from the Global Forecast System (GFS) weather variables and gridded RAVE FRP data. The model was trained on non-zero 24-hour rolling mean RAVE FRP values gridded to GFS resolution from 2019 data. Input features include latitude, longitude, various GFS meteorological variables (e.g., 10m winds, soil temperatures, precipitation, CAPE, fluxes, 2m temperature/dewpoint, etc.), a 24-hour rolling FRP average, hour of day, and a quality control flag from RAVE. Blind validation was performed on unseen fires from August-December 2021, showing improved performance over persistence (MAE: 201.81 vs. 471.38 for persistence). The model file is approximately 22.0 GB in size. The primary purpose is to enable next-hour FRP forecasting for fire-related applications using this pre-trained random forest.

Title: PM25_baseline (subfolder within the PMDA_utilities repository)
Brief Abstract: This is a subdirectory in the open-source PMDA_utilities repository, which provides utilities for the RRFS-JEDI PM2.5 Data Assimilation (PMDA) system. PMDA refers to the PM2.5 Data Assimilation component integrated into NOAA's RRFS-JEDI framework (Rapid Refresh Forecast System combined with the Joint Effort for Data assimilation - JEDI). The PM25_baseline folder specifically contains code/scripts for handling or generating baseline PM2.5 data/products. In air quality modeling and data assimilation contexts, "baseline" typically means background concentrations, prior estimates, reference fields, or non-assimilated/default PM2.5 levels used as starting points for DA experiments, bias correction, evaluation, or forecasting in the RRFS (short-range weather/air quality model).

Title: The Development of a Machine Learning Model to Predict Daily Wildfire Growth Across the Continental United States
Brief Abstract:
Wildfires burn millions of acres across the United States each year threatening human lives and property. As rapid growth occurs in the wildland-urban interface (WUI), where houses and vegetation meet, wildfires are becoming more of a pressing issue. In addition to WUI growth, climate change continues to result in a warmer and drier climate, promoting increasingly favorable conditions for wildfires. As a result, forecasting and messaging elevated wildfire potential to partners and the public is crucial. Several fire weather indices, such as the Hot-Dry-Windy index developed by Srock et al 2019, have been developed. However, these indices are either tied to a particular topographical region or composed of various different atmospheric or fuel variables. Given the disparity among fire weather indices, a need for a consolidated fire weather prediction model is needed.

In order to consolidate these forecasting indices, a machine learning model has been developed to predict daily wildfire spread across the Continental United States should a fire develop in any given location. The model accounts for 96 different atmospheric, fuel, topographical, special, and static variables such as population density, topographical slope, and regional fire climatology to predict daily wildfire growth. The resulting model shows skill in predicting areas of active fire growth out to three days in the future for new fires across the United States. This work serves as a useful foundation for predicting fire spread across spatial and temporal scales using machine learning in real time. Eventually, ML model output will allow for precise relocation of emergency resources and increase preparedness for the general public ahead of significant fire events, protecting lives and property

Title: Realtime Fire Weather Forecast and Fire Risk Visualization
Brief Abstract: The website, hosted by Texas Tech University's Atmospheric Science Group, provides real-time fire weather forecasts and fire risk visualizations specifically for the southern region. It is associated with the university's efforts in numerical weather prediction and focuses on delivering data-driven insights for fire weather conditions. For inquiries, the site lists contact information for Dr. Brian Ancell (Professor), Mr. Brandon Tomerlin, and Dr. Deepak Kumar, all affiliated with the Department of Geosciences.

Title: Red Flag Threat Index (RFTI) Visualization
Brief Abstract: This interactive web-based tool provides real-time fire weather forecasting and fire risk visualization for the Southern United States and Southern High Plains. It calculates the Red Flag Threat Index (RFTI), a composite metric used to identify critical fire weather conditions by integrating high-resolution meteorological data from the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model and machine-learning (ML) algorithms. The tool visualizes hourly RFTI values and daily fire growth potential, assisting fire managers and meteorologists in identifying areas where wind speeds, relative humidity, and fuel dryness converge to create extreme fire danger.
